Somos uma equipe movida por inovação, tecnologia e desafios. Buscamos desenvolver soluções criativas por meio da colaboração, experimentação e trabalho em equipe. Nosso processo começa com a identificação do problema, passa pela construção de ideias, divisão de responsabilidades, desenvolvimento de protótipos e testes para aprimorar as soluções.

Estamos buscando desenvolvedores, programadores e pessoas com conhecimentos em tecnologia, design, inteligência artificial e gestão de projetos.
summary:
ORBIT EXPLORE is a browser game for kids aged 7–12, in which players run Base Ares Planitia on Mars. There are five resources (Water, Food, Air, Energy and Radiation), plus Science points to buy upgrades, and every decision has a cost: making air uses water and energy, and the radiation shield drains energy every second. Random events inspired by space weather (solar storms, dust clouds) call for hard choices, and difficulty rises through three phases. When the mission fails, the game explains why and gives a tip. A panel offers facts based on DONKI and OSDR, with links to the official sources.

The project answers the challenge by turning real survival trade-offs in space into simple mechanics, with no download or account. It matters because it teaches, through play, that living off Earth means balancing limited resources against risks like radiation, bringing kids closer to science and engineering.
details:
What it is and how it works. ORBIT EXPLORE is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players run Base Ares Planitia on Mars, which starts with 2 astronauts. They must keep Water, Food, Air and Energy up while holding Radiation down. Science points, earned from experiments and by the astronauts themselves, buy 10 upgrades (water recycler, greenhouse, solar panels, shield, habitat module, antenna, ice robot, air generator, science drone and algae). Every action has a cost: melting ice, harvesting plants and researching use energy; making air (electrolysis) uses water and energy; the radiation shield drains energy every second. Random events (solar storm, solar flare, dust cloud, signal from Earth and new astronauts arriving) ask for a decision that also costs something. Difficulty rises through 3 phases over time. If water, food or air run out, or radiation passes 85%, health drops. At zero, the mission ends with an explanation of why and a tip.

Benefits. No download or account needed, runs in the browser, in plain language. Kids learn through trial and error that no choice is free and why each resource matters. Feedback is immediate, through colors (green, yellow, red) and hints.

Intended impact. To show that surviving off Earth means balancing limited resources against risks like solar radiation, which is what real mission planners do. We want to spark interest in science and engineering, at home and in the classroom. A “NASA Scientific Data” panel offers facts about space weather (DONKI) and life in space (OSDR), with links to the official sources.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, Tailwind CSS, Canvas 2D (pixel-art sky), Web Audio API (music and sounds generated in code), Google Fonts and Material Symbols. Scientific references: NASA DONKI and NASA OSDR.

Creative aspect. A retro pixel-art menu with a 1994 look, a shooting star and chiptune music generated in code. The alert bar works like a traffic light (green, yellow, red). The button the player needs at that moment pulses. Errors say which button to click. Game over is a diagnosis with a tip, not a punishment. There is an easier Explorer mode.

Factors considered. An audience of 7–12-year-olds; few resources to avoid overload; no choice without a cost; balancing fun and science (electrolysis, the shield, dust reducing solar power, radiation); replayability through random events, phases and upgrades; NASA sources credited inside the game.
